clue.text: Thing coming across perhaps from a part of N America

indicators.note: one piece coming across another spans it, so the craze word goes round the other letters

parts.note: having a thing about something is having an obsession or craze, a mania
the phrase 'from A to B' suggests that what may come after 'from a' is 'to B', giving TO B

explanation.surface: Something drifting over the border, perhaps, from a region of North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps from a' is the clever part: it calls up the phrase 'from A to B', so what follows 'from a' is supplied, and 'coming across' wraps the craze word round it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Canadian prairie province, so a part of North America.

clue.text: Note from employment cases recalled

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters are read backwards
the words act as cases that enclose the letters wanted

explanation.surface: A note from an employer about cases recalled.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'from employment' backwards and the note sits inside: (fr)OM EM(ployment) gives OMEM, which 'recalled' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A short written message is a note, especially within an office.

clue.text: Alliance vote against strike with Wellington maybe quoted

indicators.note: quoted means repeated in speech, so the words are heard

parts.words: vote against strike with Wellington maybe
parts.note: a nay is a vote against; to toe a ball is to strike it with the toe of a boot, a Wellington boot perhaps

explanation.surface: Voting against military action alongside the Duke of Wellington, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wellington' suggests the duke but means a rubber boot. 'quoted' gives the sound of NAY TOE.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance.

clue.text: Quite intoxicated with vision of fabulous creature?

parts.note: a troll is a creature of fable and folklore
eyed means having eyes, able to see

explanation.surface: So drunk you start seeing mythical monsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with vision of fabulous creature' reads as hallucination, but splits into the creature and a word for having eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for very drunk, on a par with 'legless' or 'plastered'.

clue.text: Object to pot boiler, say, about a badly brought up bouncer

indicators.note: the bird goes about, around, the other letters

parts.note: a boiler is a chicken for boiling, an example of a bird

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the letters are read from the bottom upward

parts.note: ill means badly, as in 'ill-advised'
something that bounces, like a ball (and a bouncer is a cricket delivery)

explanation.surface: Objecting to a boiler that is a poorly raised bouncer at a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' reverses A ILL to give LLIA, which 'about' wraps the bird round. A boiler is an old hen fit only for the pot; 'pot' in the definition is the snooker sense, to sink.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker or pool the cue ball strikes the coloured spheres you aim to sink in a pocket.

clue.text: As good as gold, with time securing degree in law

indicators.note: gold securing the degree holds it inside, so the law letters sit within the gold symbol

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
LLB is the Bachelor of Laws degree

explanation.surface: A law graduate who has been as good as gold, and who's held on to their degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As good as gold' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'As good as'; 'securing' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean nearly or practically, as in 'it is all but finished'.

clue.text: Dance initially brooks no mini skirts!

indicators.note: the car skirts the letter, going round it

parts.note: a limo (limousine) is the opposite of a Mini, a tiny British car

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A dance that tolerates no miniskirts at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no mini skirts' looks like a fashion ban, but the Mini is a small British car, so a limousine is no Mini; 'skirts' puts the B inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Caribbean dance in which performers lean back to pass under a low bar.

clue.text: Revolutionary action B-movies, unusually incorporating large silence

indicators.note: the shuffled letters take the other pieces into their body
unusually means arranged in an odd way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
sh is the instruction for silence

explanation.surface: Cheap films about revolution, unusually including a long period of silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' shuffles the letters of B-movies (the hyphen ignored) and 'incorporating' places the large and silence letters within them.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Russian revolutionary communism of Lenin's faction, so a revolutionary political movement.

clue.text: Relative idiot powerless to contain press

indicators.note: the remaining fool word goes round the pressing word
P is the physics symbol for power, so powerless means dropping that letter

parts.note: a twerp is a silly or idiotic person
to press is to insist, as in 'press the point'

explanation.surface: An idiot relation, now without influence, kept quiet by the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'powerless' leaves TWER once P (power) goes, and 'to contain' wraps that round the pressing word; 'press' is the verb, not newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A female sibling born at the same birth is a family member.

clue.text: One frequently walked on runs — just a bit overweight?

parts.note: a doormat or floor mat is something people walk on all the time
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs
just means only, as in 'just a little'

explanation.surface: A doormat type who is downtrodden yet runs, being only slightly overweight?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is playful: a stout, motherly figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a plump, middle-aged motherly build, so a bit overweight.

clue.text: Regularly calm, was life in Italian resort

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means every second letter of the following words, starting with the second

explanation.surface: Life was calm, as one would hope, at a holiday spot in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Every second letter of 'calm was life in' (cAlM wAs LiFe In) spells the resort; 'in' looks like a link word but provides the final I.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known town on the coast south of Naples, a classic Italian holiday destination.

clue.text: Admitted Cockney journalist, currently close to criminal, stole?

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker famously drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: a hack is a journalist
currently means now, at present

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

parts.note: edged means moved stealthily, crept or stole

explanation.surface: A London reporter, now near a criminal, crept away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cockney' drops the H from HACK, as a Londoner from the East End drops their aitches; 'stole' is the verb of creeping, not theft.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit something is to accept or concede it as true.

clue.text: In which Hants police left unrecognisable?

definitions.text: In which Hants police left unrecognisable?

indicators.note: letters made unrecognisable are disguised, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: Detectives in Hampshire go about incognito, leaving them unrecognised.
explanation.walkthrough: Hants is the short name for Hampshire, an English county with its own police force. The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Detectives working undercover wear ordinary civilian dress so the public cannot recognise them as officers.

clue.text: British offer no defence for miscreant

parts.note: to lack something is to have none of it to offer
a guard is a defence, as in 'on guard'

explanation.surface: British authorities offering no defence for a wrongdoer.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a scoundrel or villain, a wicked person.

clue.text: Tired, so given a hand when leaving?

definitions.meaning: worn out, exhausted; used especially of old machines
applauded as you go off stage

explanation.surface: A performer worn out but applauded on exit.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapped-out means worn out, and a departing performer may be applauded on the way off.

clue.text: Loaf associated with variable dough

parts.note: to loaf about is to lounge or loll
Y is a letter used for an unknown or variable in algebra

explanation.surface: A loaf of bread made from dough of varying kinds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' and 'dough' both suggest baking, but 'Loaf' is a verb (lounge) and 'dough' means money.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for money, cash.

clue.text: Type of binder is enough to hold five fliers

parts.note: a ring binder is a common kind of folder

indicators.note: the word for suffices holds the numeral inside it

parts.note: 'that does' means 'that is enough', so does = suffices
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: An office folder that has room for five sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hold' puts V inside DOES.
explanation.definitionFit: These are wood pigeons and similar birds, so things that fly.

clue.text: Female traduced by ancient works so amended

definitions.note: in Othello, Iago holds the rank of 'ancient' (an ensign) and slanders his general's wife

indicators.note: works is the anagram signal here: the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Ancient texts so amended that a woman is misrepresented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ancient works' looks like old texts, but 'ancient' is Iago's military rank in Shakespeare's Othello and 'works' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's wife is falsely accused of adultery by Iago, the ensign or 'ancient'.

clue.text: Goblet I had with singular front section in shape of lips?

parts.note: a goblet is a drinking cup
I'd is the contraction of I had
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
the bow is the front of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone describing the curve their lips made on a goblet they drank from.
explanation.definitionFit: This names the double curve of the upper lip, likened to the archer's weapon of the god of love.

clue.text: Girl turning heads in expensive, if simple, underwear and stockings

indicators.note: turning the collected letters round means reading them backwards
heads are the first letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A girl turning heads in lingerie and stockings that are pricey though plain.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of 'expensive if simple underwear stockings' are EISUS; 'turning' reads them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female first name, a pet form of Susan.

clue.text: Old air shelter among places for putting underwear briefly

indicators.note: the shelter word goes among the other pieces, between them

parts.note: golfers putt on the greens

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a vest is an undershirt in British English
lee is shelter from the wind

explanation.surface: A shelter on a golf course for storing underclothes, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts the last letter, leaving VES, and 'among' sets the shelter between the golf and underwear pieces. Vest here is the British undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional English folk tune dating from Tudor times, so an old song.

clue.text: Name for top of steel tower where ladder can appear?

indicators.note: the name letter replaces the first letter of the tower

parts.note: a pylon is a steel tower carrying power lines

explanation.surface: A name for the top of a steel tower where a ladder could be placed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ladder' looks like climbing gear, but it is a run in a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockings and tights are made of this synthetic fabric, which can get a ladder, a run.

clue.text: Scoop has leading couple turning up to it

indicators.note: the first two letters swap round, turning about

parts.note: to bale is to scoop water out of a boat

explanation.surface: A news scoop with the leading pair turning up to report it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading couple turning' swaps only the first two letters of BALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up to it means having the capacity or competence to do something.

clue.text: Peer gleefully if vacantly over book collection

indicators.note: vacantly means emptied of its inside, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: NT, the New Testament, is a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone peering gleefully, if blankly, at a collection of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a verb (to look) but is the first name of Ibsen's hero; this is his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibsen's verse play is named after its hero Peer, so this word completes his name.

clue.text: Programme targeting satellite audience initially to get disastrous ratings?

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of the word that follows

parts.note: a poll (survey of opinion or ratings) of O, zero, would be a disaster

explanation.surface: A TV show about satellites whose audience figures are a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Programme' suggests television, but it is a space programme; the satellite is the Moon.
explanation.definitionFit: The NASA space effort that landed astronauts on the Moon, Earth's natural satellite.

clue.text: After exchanges, do you bag some bargain?

indicators.note: letters that exchange places are rearranged

explanation.surface: A shopper asking whether you grab a bargain after swapping goods.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Some bargain!' is an exclamation praising a purchase that was worth the money.

clue.text: Cook reduced flavour (that's no longer all there)

parts.note: to do food is to cook it, as in 'do the potatoes'

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a tinge is a slight flavour or trace

explanation.surface: A cook reducing a sauce whose flavour has partly gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' takes E off TINGE. 'Cook' and 'reduced' suggest the kitchen, but the definition is about a failing mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone senile or in their dotage has lost some of their faculties, so is no longer all there.

clue.text: Touching article on radio presenter — a change from Us hosts

parts.note: A is the indefinite article
a DJ (disc jockey) presents music on radio
a cent is small change in the US

explanation.surface: A radio presenter as host for once, moving from US broadcasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Things side by side are next to each other, in contact.
